questions.text: In the IBC Section 506.2 frontage increase formula, what is the minimum F/P (frontage-to-perimeter) ratio required for ANY frontage increase to apply, and what is the maximum value of the frontage increase factor (If)?

options.text: F/P must exceed 0.25 (25%); maximum If = 0.75
F/P must equal 0.50 (50%); maximum If = 1.00
F/P must exceed 0.15 (15%); maximum If = 0.50
F/P must exceed 0.30 (30%); maximum If = 0.60

questions.rationale: These two numerical thresholds are frequently tested. The 0.25 (25%) threshold is the qualifying floor — below it, no increase. The 0.75 (75%) cap prevents the frontage bonus from dominating the calculation. Both are hard limits that must be memorized.

questions.text: A service drop (≤600V) passes over the flat roof of a commercial building. Per PD 1096, Rule XIII, Section 1301, what is the minimum required vertical clearance above the roof surface?
questions.rationale: The 2.50 m roof clearance reflects the maximum height a person standing on a flat roof could reach while still maintaining safe distance from the service drop conductor. The two exceptions (1.00 m for sloped roofs, 500 mm for small overhangs ≤ 1.20 m) account for situations where the service drop crosses a pitched surface or a minor roof protrusion where the risk profile is different.

questions.text: Per PD 1096, Rule XIII, Section 1302, at what minimum height above the floor must a window-type air conditioning unit be installed when it discharges into a public area?
questions.rationale: The 2.10 m minimum is calibrated to place the discharge air above the head height of standing adults while remaining accessible for maintenance. It also positions the condensate drain above the floor level to prevent water accumulation in occupied spaces.

questions.text: Using the 'SALLIE' mnemonic for the five core principles of Rule XVIII, which of the following correctly assigns each letter to its corresponding principle?

options.text: S = Scope; A = Area limits; L = Light; L = Louvered windows; I = Impact; E = Exceptions
S = Strength; A = Area limits; L = Lighting; L = Louvered windows; I = Impact; E = Exceptions
S = Safety; A = Area limits; L = Length limits; L = Louvered windows; I = Insulation; E = Exceptions
S = Scope; A = Anchors; L = Light; L = Louvered; I = Impact; E = Energy efficiency

questions.rationale: Using SALLIE at the start of any Rule XVIII question ensures all five sections are considered. The mnemonic is particularly valuable for distinguishing between Section 1802 (area limits and safety glass triggers) and Section 1805 (impact requirements and exceptions), which are the most frequently confused provisions.

questions.text: Under Section 1805, Exception 2 (bottom edge ≥ 450 mm above floor), IBC 2021, and CPSC 16 CFR Part 1201, compare the Philippine code's height threshold for the floor-proximity exception to the US standards.

options.text: PH: ≥ 450 mm; IBC: ≥ 457 mm (18 in); CPSC: Category I < 0.84 sq.m / 150 ft-lbs; Category II ≥ 0.84 sq.m / 400 ft-lbs
PH: ≥ 600 mm; IBC: ≥ 610 mm (24 in); CPSC: Category I < 1.00 sq.m / 200 ft-lbs; Category II ≥ 1.00 sq.m / 500 ft-lbs
PH: ≥ 450 mm; IBC: ≥ 300 mm (12 in); CPSC: No energy-based classification
PH: ≥ 300 mm; IBC: ≥ 457 mm (18 in); CPSC: Category I < 0.84 sq.m / 150 ft-lbs; Category II ≥ 0.84 sq.m / 400 ft-lbs

questions.rationale: The PH (450 mm) and IBC (457 mm) thresholds are functionally equivalent — the 7 mm difference is a rounding artifact of imperial-to-metric conversion. The CPSC energy classification (150 ft-lbs vs 400 ft-lbs) has no PH equivalent.

questions.text: From what point is the Building Height Limit (BHL) measured, and to what point is it measured?

options.text: From the highest adjacent grade to the topmost portion of the building, ensuring compliance with zoning regulations
From the established grade line to the topmost portion of the building
From the lowest adjoining ground to the eave line, which affects the overall silhouette of the structure
From the first floor slab to the parapet wall, defining the vertical extent of the building

questions.rationale: The established grade line is not necessarily the lowest or highest point of the lot — it is a defined reference plane. On sloping sites, special rules apply (3-meter tolerance rule).

questions.text: A tower spire made of combustible materials extends above the roof of a building. What is the maximum height above the prescribed BHL that this spire may extend?

options.text: Spires of combustible materials are not permitted above BHL

questions.rationale: This exemption allows decorative and functional rooftop elements without penalizing the building's height compliance, subject to structural safety and aviation requirements.

questions.text: A commercial lot is served by a single RROW that is 5.00 m wide. The occupancy-based BHL for the use is 20.00 m. What BHL cap applies in practice?

options.text: 20.00 m, since the occupancy-based BHL governs
9.00 m (approximately 3 storeys)
7.50 m (approximately 2.5 storeys)
6.00 m (approximately 2 storeys)

questions.rationale: The RROW override creates three bands: 6–7m RROW → ~3 storeys/9m; 4–5m RROW → ~2.5 storeys/7.5m; ≤3m RROW → ~2 storeys/6m. These caps override any higher occupancy-based BHL.

questions.text: On a sloping site, by how much may the building height measured from the lowest adjoining ground exceed the prescribed BHL without penalty?

options.text: No tolerance — the BHL is absolute from the lowest point

questions.rationale: The 3-meter tolerance recognizes that requiring all points on a sloped lot to meet the BHL exactly would create impractical design constraints on hillsides.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, Section 707, what is the THREE independent development controls that must all be satisfied simultaneously?

options.text: BHL, PSO, and TGFA
BHL, FLAR, and PSO
BHL, AMBF, and TOSL
BHL, GFA, and TOSL

questions.rationale: These three controls are independent — a high FLAR does not mean high BHL, and high PSO does not mean high FLAR. On the exam, all three apply simultaneously and the most restrictive result must be adopted.

questions.text: A factory floor measures 20 m × 15 m with a 4.00 m ceiling. Under PD 1096 Rule VIII, Section 807, what is the maximum legal occupancy for this workshop?

options.text: 50 workers
100 workers
120 workers
200 workers

questions.rationale: This calculation demonstrates how ceiling height directly affects maximum occupancy. A developer who lowers a workshop ceiling from 4.00 m to 2.70 m reduces legal occupancy from 100 to 67 workers — a 33% reduction. Rule VIII minimums protect against exactly this kind of cost-driven compression.

questions.text: The four mental buckets of Rule VIII organize the rule into which categories, and what are their corresponding anchor phrases?

options.text: The Footprint (minimum room sizes — '6-3-1.2 / 2-1.5-0.9'); The Volume (ceiling heights — 'Natural 2.70; AC 2.40; multi-storey cascades'); The Lungs (window openings and courts — '10% rooms, special rule for baths'); The Atmosphere (air space per person — '3-12-14: School–Work–Home')

The Footprint (minimum ceiling heights, which are crucial for ventilation); The Volume (minimum room sizes, ensuring adequate space); The Lungs (air space per person, which is essential for health); The Atmosphere (window openings, providing natural light)

The Footprint (floor area ratios, which dictate building density); The Volume (room volumes, affecting acoustics); The Lungs (vent shaft dimensions, crucial for air circulation); The Atmosphere (HVAC requirements, ensuring thermal comfort)

The Footprint (minimum setbacks, which affect urban density); The Volume (ceiling heights, impacting room proportions); The Lungs (court dimensions, necessary for light access); The Atmosphere (property line requirements, which influence privacy)

questions.rationale: Organizing Rule VIII into four buckets is an exam strategy: the rule covers four distinct aspects of the built environment (footprint/area, vertical dimension/height, air supply/windows, air volume/person). When answering any Rule VIII question, immediately identify which bucket it belongs to, then retrieve the relevant section and numbers.

questions.text: A contractor installs a canopy walkway over a temporary pedestrian path. Materials including sandbags and steel formwork are stored on top of the canopy deck. Under PD 1096 Rule XI, Section 1106(d), what is required regarding the canopy's curb board?

options.text: At least 150 mm high and tight, ensuring no materials fall off the edges
At least 200 mm high on the street side only, which may not provide full protection
At least 300 mm high and tight on all edges where materials are stored
At least 450 mm high and tight, providing maximum safety against material displacement

questions.rationale: The canopy addresses the most serious hazard: falling objects from height. The 2.40 m clear height (underneath) and the 300 mm curb board (on top) work together — one protects headroom, the other prevents objects from rolling or being kicked off.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule XI, Section 1106(d), what is the minimum clear height required for a canopy walkway above the temporary pedestrian path surface?

options.text: 1.80 meters
2.00 meters
2.40 meters
3.00 meters

questions.rationale: The 2.40 m figure appears twice in Rule XI: as the fence height (above grade) and as the canopy clear height (above walkway surface). The candidate must identify which dimension applies to which structure. The mnemonic '1-6-1-2-2-3' covers walkway (1.20 m), railing (1.00 m), fence (2.40 m), canopy clear (2.40 m), and curb board (300 mm).

questions.text: An architect specifies plastic skylights on a flat-roofed commercial building with roof slope less than 1:4. Under PD 1096 Section 1607, what is the minimum required curb height at the perimeter of each skylight?

options.text: 50 mm
100 mm
150 mm
300 mm

questions.rationale: The 100 mm curb requirement applies to flat roofs (slope < 1:4). The wire screen alternative (No. 12 gauge, 25 mm mesh) serves the same purpose — preventing burning material from falling through a failed skylight.

questions.text: Per PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1209, exterior balconies, landings, and porches at what minimum height above grade require railings of incombustible material?

options.text: More than 450 mm above grade
More than 600 mm above grade
More than 750 mm above grade
More than 1,000 mm above grade

questions.rationale: Per Rule XII, Sec. 1209, exterior balconies, landings, and porches more than 750 mm above grade must have railings of incombustible materials. Below 750 mm, the incombustible requirement does not apply and any material permitted by the Type of Construction may be used. This is a critical trap: the incombustible railing requirement applies only above 750 mm.

questions.text: Per PD 1096 Rule XII, Sec. 1210.b, a compliant penthouse is excluded from Building Height Limit (BHL) calculations. Under what condition does it lose this exclusion?

options.text: When the penthouse area exceeds 200 sq.m, including any additional mechanical spaces
When the penthouse height exceeds 3.60 m (or 8.40 m for elevator/tank enclosures), measured from the finished floor level
When the penthouse is used for any purpose other than sheltering mechanical equipment or enclosing shaft openings
When the supporting roof is more than 50 m above grade, considering the highest point of the structure

questions.rationale: A code-compliant penthouse (within height limits, within 1/3 area, and used only for permitted purposes) is excluded from BHL. If the penthouse is used for prohibited purposes (habitable, commercial, or residential use), it is reclassified as an additional storey and loses the BHL exclusion — its full height is added to the regulated building height.

questions.text: Per PD 1096, Rule IX, Sec. 906, what governs the specific numerical noise level standards?

options.text: PD 1096 itself sets specific dB limits, which are detailed in supplementary guidelines issued by the local government units
PD 984 (Pollution Control Law) and DENR Administrative Orders on ambient noise standards
WHO guidelines are directly enforceable under PD 1096, as they are incorporated by reference into national standards
Noise standards are set by the Municipal Health Officer, who has the authority to adjust limits based on local environmental conditions

questions.rationale: Per Rule IX, Sec. 906, PD 1096 requires adequate noise abatement devices but does not specify numerical limits. Those are governed by PD 984 (Pollution Control Law) and DENR Administrative Orders. Architects use ASHRAE NC ratings as design targets.

questions.text: Per the memory aid 'GPRW' for sign types, what do the letters stand for?

options.text: General, Projecting, Roof, Wall
Ground, Projecting, Roof, Wall
Graphic, Portable, Regulatory, Warning
Ground, Panel, Regulatory, Wall

questions.rationale: GPRW = Ground Signs (within property line, height per LZR); Projecting Signs (≤1.00 m / flush, ≥3.00 m/5.00 m clearance); Roof Signs (no wood, ground it, light it for aircraft); Wall Signs (≤300 mm projection, ≥3.00 m clearance, flush/recessed ≤3 m).

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, combustible decorative spires, towers, and similar architectural elements may exceed the BHL by what maximum height?

options.text: Combustible spires may extend up to 3 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires may extend up to 6 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires may extend up to 9 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires are not permitted to exceed the BHL under any circumstance

questions.rationale: Rule VII permits combustible decorative spires, towers, and similar non-occupiable architectural elements to extend up to 6 meters above the Building Height Limit, provided they are not used for occupancy or storage.
questions.explanation: The 6-meter allowance for combustible spires recognizes the aesthetic and cultural importance of decorative vertical elements such as church steeples, traditional towers, and architectural finials. The restriction to non-occupiable, non-storage elements ensures that the fire safety intent of the BHL is not compromised by habitable space above the limit.

questions.text: PD 1096 Rule VII allows a tolerance for buildings on sloping sites. What is the maximum additional height tolerance permitted above the BHL for buildings on sloping lots?

options.text: 1.5 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
2.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
3.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
5.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions

questions.rationale: Rule VII allows a 3-meter tolerance above the BHL for buildings on sloping sites. This tolerance accommodates the natural grade change across a sloping lot without penalizing buildings that are not artificially leveled.
questions.explanation: The 3-meter sloping site tolerance reflects the practical reality that measuring building height from a single datum on a site with significant grade changes can produce inequitable results. A building that steps down a slope may appear taller at its lower end even though its design respects the BHL at the main entrance datum.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, from what datum is the Building Height Limit (BHL) measured?

options.text: From the lowest finished floor level of the building
From the established grade at the building's main entrance
From the established grade at the midpoint of the lot frontage
From the crown of the nearest public road adjacent to the lot

questions.rationale: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, the Building Height Limit is measured from the established grade at the building's main entrance. This datum ensures a consistent measurement baseline referenced to the primary access point of the building.
questions.explanation: The main entrance grade datum prevents manipulation of BHL calculations by choosing the lowest point on a sloping site as the measurement base. Using the main entrance grade anchors the height measurement to the most publicly visible and accessible face of the building.

questions.text: A building lot fronts on a 3-meter-wide road. The designer proposes a 3-storey building. Applying PD 1096 Rule VII RROW-based storey caps, which statement correctly evaluates this proposal?

options.text: Non-compliant: a 3-meter RROW limits the building to 2 storeys maximum
Compliant: a 3-meter RROW permits up to 2.5 storeys, and 3 storeys rounds within this range
Non-compliant: a 3-meter RROW prohibits any multi-storey construction
Compliant: RROW width caps apply only to commercial buildings, not residential designs

questions.rationale: Rule VII specifies that an RROW of 3 meters or less limits buildings to a maximum of 2 storeys. A proposed 3-storey building on a 3-meter RROW exceeds this cap and is non-compliant regardless of compliance with BHL or FLAR.
questions.explanation: The RROW storey cap is a hard limit, not subject to rounding or interpretation. A 3-meter RROW places the lot in the '3 meters or less' category with a 2-storey maximum. The designer cannot argue that 3 storeys 'approximates' 2.5 storeys. The 2.5-storey tier requires a 4–5 meter RROW. The 3-meter lot must be designed as a 2-storey building maximum.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, a lot fronts on a road right-of-way (RROW) with a width of 5 meters. What is the maximum number of storeys permitted for a building on this lot based on RROW width alone?

options.text: 2 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
2.5 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
3 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
No storey limit applies based solely on RROW width

questions.rationale: Rule VII specifies RROW-based storey caps: RROWs of 6–7 meters permit 3 storeys; RROWs of 4–5 meters permit 2.5 storeys; RROWs of 3 meters or less permit 2 storeys. A 5-meter RROW falls in the 4–5 meter range, limiting the building to 2.5 storeys.
questions.explanation: The RROW-based storey cap is one of three independent height controls in Rule VII (alongside BHL and FLAR). It ensures that building height is proportional to the width of the access road, maintaining adequate light, air, and emergency access. A 5-meter RROW is in the middle tier (4–5m = 2.5 storeys), not the upper tier (6–7m = 3 storeys).

questions.text: Rule VII establishes three independent development controls that simultaneously govern building height and bulk. Which statement correctly describes their relationship?

options.text: BHL, FLAR, and PSO are additive: satisfying any two of the three is sufficient for compliance
BHL governs height while FLAR and PSO govern bulk; only the most restrictive of the latter two applies
BHL, FLAR, and PSO are independent controls; the building must comply with all three simultaneously
FLAR supersedes BHL when FLAR calculations produce a lower building volume than the BHL allows

questions.rationale: Under Rule VII, Building Height Limit (BHL), Floor to Lot Area Ratio (FLAR), and Percentage of Site Occupancy (PSO) are three independent development controls. A building must satisfy all three simultaneously — satisfying two out of three is insufficient for compliance.
questions.explanation: The three-control system is intentionally redundant: a building could be within the BHL (height) but still violate FLAR (total floor area relative to lot) or PSO (footprint coverage). In practice, the most restrictive control often determines the actual buildable envelope. All three must pass — there is no provision for trading compliance in one control for non-compliance in another.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, what is the correct definition of Gross Floor Area (GFA) as distinguished from Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA)?

options.text: GFA includes all floor areas including parking, utilities, and service areas; TGFA excludes these, which is contrary to standard practice
GFA is the usable floor area of a single storey; TGFA is the sum of GFA across all storeys of the building
GFA and TGFA are interchangeable terms referring to total building floor area, which is a common misconception
GFA excludes basement areas; TGFA includes basement floor area in the total, which is not typically the case

questions.rationale: Under Rule VII, GFA is the gross floor area of a single storey, while TGFA (Total Gross Floor Area) is the sum of GFA across all storeys of the entire building. FLAR is calculated using TGFA divided by lot area.
questions.explanation: The GFA/TGFA distinction is critical for FLAR calculations. FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area. Using a single storey's GFA instead of the total TGFA would produce a dramatically understated FLAR value. Architects must sum the GFA of every storey — including basement, ground, and all upper floors — to arrive at the TGFA used in FLAR compliance checks.

questions.text: A lot with an area of 600 sq.m is in a zone with a prescribed FLAR of 3.0. What is the maximum Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) permitted for a building on this lot?

options.text: 600 square meters maximum TGFA
1,200 square meters maximum TGFA
1,800 square meters maximum TGFA
2,400 square meters maximum TGFA

questions.rationale: FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area. Rearranging: TGFA = FLAR × Lot Area = 3.0 × 600 sq.m = 1,800 sq.m. The maximum permitted Total Gross Floor Area is 1,800 square meters.
questions.explanation: The FLAR formula is TGFA = FLAR × Lot Area. With FLAR 3.0 on a 600 sq.m lot: 3.0 × 600 = 1,800 sq.m TGFA maximum. This represents the upper bound of total building floor area — the actual achievable TGFA may be less if BHL or PSO limits constrain the design first.

questions.text: A building's TGFA is 2,400 sq.m on a lot of 800 sq.m. The prescribed maximum FLAR for the zone is 2.8. Is this building compliant with the FLAR control?

options.text: Compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which is within the 2.8 maximum
Non-compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which exceeds the 2.8 maximum
Compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which rounds down to 2.8 within tolerance
Non-compliant: TGFA of 2,400 sq.m exceeds the 800 sq.m lot area and is automatically non-compliant

questions.rationale: FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area = 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0. The computed FLAR of 3.0 exceeds the prescribed maximum of 2.8. The building is non-compliant with the FLAR control regardless of BHL or PSO compliance.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic is clean: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0, which is above the 2.8 limit. There is no rounding provision in the code — 3.0 exceeds 2.8 precisely. The maximum compliant TGFA would be 2.8 × 800 = 2,240 sq.m. The building as designed exceeds this by 160 sq.m and must reduce total floor area to comply.

questions.text: A 500 sq.m lot in a residential zone has a prescribed FLAR of 2.0, a PSO of 60%, and a BHL of 10 meters. The architect proposes a 3-storey building with a 300 sq.m footprint per floor (TGFA = 900 sq.m). Evaluate compliance with all three Rule VII controls.

options.text: All three controls are satisfied: FLAR 1.8 < 2.0, PSO 60% = 60%, BHL subject to storey height confirmation
Two controls satisfied; PSO is violated because 300 sq.m footprint on 500 sq.m lot equals 60%, exactly at the limit
FLAR is violated: 900 sq.m TGFA on 500 sq.m lot = FLAR 1.8, which exceeds 2.0 maximum
All three controls are violated: FLAR 1.8 exceeds 2.0, PSO 60% exceeds the limit, and BHL requires verification

questions.rationale: FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area = 900 ÷ 500 = 1.8, which is below the 2.0 maximum. PSO = Footprint ÷ Lot Area = 300 ÷ 500 = 60%, which equals (not exceeds) the 60% maximum. BHL compliance depends on storey height but is potentially satisfied at 10m for 3 storeys. All three controls are met or within limits.
questions.explanation: Three simultaneous calculations: (1) FLAR = 900 ÷ 500 = 1.8 ≤ 2.0 — compliant; (2) PSO = 300 ÷ 500 = 0.60 = 60% — exactly at the limit, which is compliant (the limit is a maximum, not a value to be exceeded); (3) BHL at 10m for 3 storeys — typical floor-to-floor heights of 3.0–3.3m would yield 9.0–9.9m for 3 storeys, within 10m. Option C contains a math error (1.8 < 2.0, not greater). Option B mischaracterizes 'exactly at the limit' as a violation.

questions.text: A building's TGFA is 2,400 sq.m on a lot of 800 sq.m. The prescribed maximum FLAR for the zone is 2.8. Is this building compliant with the FLAR control?

options.text: Compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which is within the 2.8 maximum
Non-compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which exceeds the 2.8 maximum
Compliant: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0 FLAR, which rounds down to 2.8 within tolerance
Non-compliant: TGFA of 2,400 sq.m exceeds the 800 sq.m lot area and is automatically non-compliant

questions.rationale: FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area = 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0. The computed FLAR of 3.0 exceeds the prescribed maximum of 2.8. The building is non-compliant with the FLAR control regardless of BHL or PSO compliance.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic is clean: 2,400 ÷ 800 = 3.0, which is above the 2.8 limit. There is no rounding provision in the code — 3.0 exceeds 2.8 precisely. The maximum compliant TGFA would be 2.8 × 800 = 2,240 sq.m. The building as designed exceeds this by 160 sq.m and must reduce total floor area to comply.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, what is the correct definition of Gross Floor Area (GFA) as distinguished from Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA)?

options.text: GFA includes all floor areas including parking, utilities, and service areas; TGFA excludes these, which affects the calculation of building density
GFA is the usable floor area of a single storey; TGFA is the sum of GFA across all storeys of the building
GFA and TGFA are interchangeable terms referring to total building floor area, though this is a common misconception
GFA excludes basement areas; TGFA includes basement floor area in the total, impacting the overall building footprint

questions.rationale: Under Rule VII, GFA is the gross floor area of a single storey, while TGFA (Total Gross Floor Area) is the sum of GFA across all storeys of the entire building. FLAR is calculated using TGFA divided by lot area.
questions.explanation: The GFA/TGFA distinction is critical for FLAR calculations. FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area. Using a single storey's GFA instead of the total TGFA would produce a dramatically understated FLAR value. Architects must sum the GFA of every storey — including basement, ground, and all upper floors — to arrive at the TGFA used in FLAR compliance checks.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, from what datum is the Building Height Limit (BHL) measured?

options.text: From the lowest finished floor level of the building
From the established grade at the building's main entrance
From the established grade at the midpoint of the lot frontage
From the crown of the nearest public road adjacent to the lot

questions.rationale: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, the Building Height Limit is measured from the established grade at the building's main entrance. This datum ensures a consistent measurement baseline referenced to the primary access point of the building.
questions.explanation: The main entrance grade datum prevents manipulation of BHL calculations by choosing the lowest point on a sloping site as the measurement base. Using the main entrance grade anchors the height measurement to the most publicly visible and accessible face of the building.

options.text: Non-compliant: a 3-meter RROW limits the building to 2 storeys maximum
Compliant: a 3-meter RROW permits up to 2.5 storeys, and 3 storeys rounds within this range
Non-compliant: a 3-meter RROW prohibits any multi-storey construction
Compliant: RROW width caps apply only to commercial buildings, not residential designs

BHL compliance depends on storey height but is potentially satisfied at 10m for 3 storeys. All three controls are met or within limits.

Option C contains a math error (1.8 < 2.0, not greater). Option B mischaracterizes 'exactly at the limit' as a violation.

questions.text: A lot with an area of 600 sq.m is in a zone with a prescribed FLAR of 3.0. What is the maximum Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) permitted for a building on this lot?

options.text: 600 square meters maximum TGFA
1,200 square meters maximum TGFA
1,800 square meters maximum TGFA
2,400 square meters maximum TGFA

questions.rationale: FLAR = TGFA ÷ Lot Area. Rearranging: TGFA = FLAR × Lot Area = 3.0 × 600 sq.m = 1,800 sq.m. The maximum permitted Total Gross Floor Area is 1,800 square meters.
questions.explanation: The FLAR formula is TGFA = FLAR × Lot Area. With FLAR 3.0 on a 600 sq.m lot: 3.0 × 600 = 1,800 sq.m TGFA maximum. This represents the upper bound of total building floor area — the actual achievable TGFA may be less if BHL or PSO limits constrain the design first.

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, a lot fronts on a road right-of-way (RROW) with a width of 5 meters. What is the maximum number of storeys permitted for a building on this lot based on RROW width alone?

options.text: 2 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
2.5 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
3 storeys maximum for an RROW of 5 meters
No storey limit applies based solely on RROW width

questions.rationale: Rule VII specifies RROW-based storey caps: RROWs of 6–7 meters permit 3 storeys; RROWs of 4–5 meters permit 2.5 storeys; RROWs of 3 meters or less permit 2 storeys. A 5-meter RROW falls in the 4–5 meter range, limiting the building to 2.5 storeys.
questions.explanation: The RROW-based storey cap is one of three independent height controls in Rule VII (alongside BHL and FLAR). It ensures that building height is proportional to the width of the access road, maintaining adequate light, air, and emergency access. A 5-meter RROW is in the middle tier (4–5m = 2.5 storeys), not the upper tier (6–7m = 3 storeys).

questions.text: Under PD 1096 Rule VII, combustible decorative spires, towers, and similar architectural elements may exceed the BHL by what maximum height?

options.text: Combustible spires may extend up to 3 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires may extend up to 6 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires may extend up to 9 meters above the BHL
Combustible spires are not permitted to exceed the BHL under any circumstance

questions.rationale: Rule VII permits combustible decorative spires, towers, and similar non-occupiable architectural elements to extend up to 6 meters above the Building Height Limit, provided they are not used for occupancy or storage.
questions.explanation: The 6-meter allowance for combustible spires recognizes the aesthetic and cultural importance of decorative vertical elements such as church steeples, traditional towers, and architectural finials. The restriction to non-occupiable, non-storage elements ensures that the fire safety intent of the BHL is not compromised by habitable space above the limit.

questions.text: Rule VII establishes three independent development controls that simultaneously govern building height and bulk. Which statement correctly describes their relationship?

options.text: BHL, FLAR, and PSO are additive: satisfying any two of the three is sufficient for compliance
BHL governs height while FLAR and PSO govern bulk; only the most restrictive of the latter two applies
BHL, FLAR, and PSO are independent controls; the building must comply with all three simultaneously
FLAR supersedes BHL when FLAR calculations produce a lower building volume than the BHL allows

questions.rationale: Under Rule VII, Building Height Limit (BHL), Floor to Lot Area Ratio (FLAR), and Percentage of Site Occupancy (PSO) are three independent development controls. A building must satisfy all three simultaneously — satisfying two out of three is insufficient for compliance.
questions.explanation: The three-control system is intentionally redundant: a building could be within the BHL (height) but still violate FLAR (total floor area relative to lot) or PSO (footprint coverage). In practice, the most restrictive control often determines the actual buildable envelope. All three must pass — there is no provision for trading compliance in one control for non-compliance in another.

questions.text: PD 1096 Rule VII allows a tolerance for buildings on sloping sites. What is the maximum additional height tolerance permitted above the BHL for buildings on sloping lots?

options.text: 1.5 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
2.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
3.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions
5.0 meters additional tolerance for sloping site conditions

questions.rationale: Rule VII allows a 3-meter tolerance above the BHL for buildings on sloping sites. This tolerance accommodates the natural grade change across a sloping lot without penalizing buildings that are not artificially leveled.
questions.explanation: The 3-meter sloping site tolerance reflects the practical reality that measuring building height from a single datum on a site with significant grade changes can produce inequitable results. A building that steps down a slope may appear taller at its lower end even though its design respects the BHL at the main entrance datum.
